unit.title: 3D Shapes
unit.blurb: Faces, edges and vertices of 3D shapes, nets of cubes, prisms and pyramids, and the difference between capacity and volume.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Identify and describe 3D shapes by their faces, edges and vertices, and recognise their nets.

O2.t: Understand the difference between capacity and volume, and find the volume of cuboids by counting cubes.

lesson.t: What are faces, edges and vertices?
p: A **face** is a flat or curved surface of a 3D shape. An **edge** is where two faces meet. A **vertex** (plural **vertices**) is a corner where edges meet.
A **prism** has the **same cross-section all the way through** and two identical, parallel ends. A triangular prism has triangles at both ends.
A **pyramid** has a flat base and triangular faces that meet at a point (the apex). It is named after its base: square-based pyramid.
A **net** is a flat 2D shape that **folds up** to make a 3D shape.
A cube has 11 different nets. Each is made of 6 squares, and when folded no two squares may overlap.
To check a net, imagine folding it: pick one face as the base and fold the others up around it.

lesson.t: How do I check if a net makes a cube?
p: Step 1: Count the squares – there must be 6.
Step 2: No more than 4 squares may be in one straight line.
Step 3: Pick a base and fold up the sides in your head: each face must land on a different side.
Step 4: If two squares would land on the same side, it is not a net.

lesson.q: How many faces, edges and vertices does a pentagonal prism have?
A net has 2 triangles and 3 rectangles. What 3D shape does it make?
steps: 2 identical triangle ends + rectangles joining them

p: Do not forget the edges and vertices you cannot see in a drawing. Use the table or a real shape to check.
For shapes with flat faces: **faces + vertices − edges = 2**. Cube: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2 ✓. Use it to check your counts.

lesson.t: What is the difference between capacity and volume?
p: **Volume** is the amount of **space a 3D object takes up**. It is measured in **cubic units**: cm³, m³.
**Capacity** is the amount a container can **hold**, usually of a liquid. It is measured in **millilitres (ml)** and **litres (l)**.
**1 cm³ = 1 ml** and **1000 cm³ = 1 litre**.

lesson.t: How do I find the volume of a cuboid?
p: Count the cubes: a cuboid 4 cubes long, 3 wide and 2 high has 4 × 3 = 12 cubes in each layer and 2 layers: 24 cubes.
So **volume of a cuboid = length × width × height**. A box 5 cm by 4 cm by 3 cm has volume 60 cm³.

lesson.t: How do I find the volume by counting cubes?
p: Step 1: Count the cubes along the length and the width of the bottom layer and multiply.
Step 2: Count how many layers there are.
Step 3: Multiply: cubes per layer × number of layers.
Step 4: Write the units (cm³ for centimetre cubes).

lesson.q: A cuboid is 6 cm long, 2 cm wide and 4 cm high. Find its volume.
A fish tank is 50 cm by 20 cm by 30 cm. How many litres of water can it hold?

p: Volume multiplies the three lengths; it is not 6 + 2 + 4. Also, area is cm² and volume is cm³.
If you cannot remember the formula, picture the cuboid as layers of cubes. It always works.
